title: 5-Day Python for Data Analysis
expected_outcome: You can load a messy CSV, clean it, compute grouped statistics, plot the results, and explain what the numbers mean.
milestones: Day 2: comfortable with NumPy arrays and vectorised maths
Day 4: produce a clean multi-panel chart from raw data
Day 5: ship a small end-to-end analysis notebook

days.topic_title: Python setup, syntax and data structures
days.concept_explanation: Set up a virtual environment and a notebook, then practise the four structures you will use every day: lists, dictionaries, sets and generators. The goal is fluency, not theory: you should be able to transform a list of records without looking things up.
key_takeaways: A virtual environment keeps project packages separate from the system Python.
Dictionary and list comprehensions replace most short loops.
Generators stream data instead of loading it all into memory.

resources.title: Python Tutorial: Data Structures
resources.relevance_note: Canonical reference for lists, dicts, sets and comprehensions.

resources.title: Python for Beginners (search)
resources.relevance_note: Pick one long-form course and follow along in your own editor.

practice_exercises: Create a virtual environment, install pandas, and confirm the import works.
Parse a list of 'name,score' strings into a dictionary of scores with a comprehension.
days.assignment: Write a script that reads a list of log lines and counts how often each status code appears, using collections.Counter.
days.revision_checkpoint: Why is a dictionary lookup O(1) while a list search is O(n)?

days.concept_explanation: NumPy stores numbers in one contiguous block instead of a list of objects, which is why operations run 50-100x faster. Learn shapes, slicing, broadcasting and boolean masks. Most pandas performance comes from these primitives.
key_takeaways: Vectorised operations replace Python loops for numeric work.
Broadcasting stretches compatible shapes without copying data.
Boolean masks filter arrays faster than manual loops.

resources.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
resources.relevance_note: Short, practical introduction with runnable examples.

practice_exercises: Normalise a 5x5 random matrix to the 0-1 range using array maths only.
Compute pairwise Euclidean distance between two point arrays without a for loop.
days.assignment: Compute a 7-point moving average over a noisy signal using np.convolve.
days.revision_checkpoint: What shape does broadcasting produce for arrays of shape (4,1) and (1,3)?

days.concept_explanation: A DataFrame is a set of typed columns. Today is about the three operations that cover most real work: select the right rows, fix missing values, and aggregate by group. Learn to chain them so the pipeline reads top to bottom.
key_takeaways: Use .loc for label-based selection and .iloc for positions.
groupby().agg() is a split-apply-combine in one line.
Decide on missing-value policy before you aggregate, not after.

resources.title: Pandas user guide: group by
resources.relevance_note: Covers aggregation, transformation and filtering by group.

practice_exercises: Load a CSV, inspect dtypes, and convert a date column with pd.to_datetime.
Fill missing numeric values with the median per category.
days.assignment: Take a retail sales CSV and produce revenue per region per month, sorted descending.
days.revision_checkpoint: When does .query() read better than a boolean mask, and when does it not?

days.concept_explanation: A chart exists to answer one question. Choose the mark (bar, line, scatter) from the question, not from habit. Then strip everything that does not help: gridlines, legends for one series, and titles that restate the axis.
key_takeaways: Distributions first, then relationships, then comparisons.
Sort bars by value; unsorted bars hide the ranking.
Label units on the axis, not in the title.

resources.title: Matplotlib: anatomy of a figure
resources.relevance_note: Explains figures, axes and artists so you can control layout.

practice_exercises: Build a 1x3 panel: histogram, box plot and scatter for one dataset.
Recreate one chart from a news article and list what you changed.
days.assignment: Chart the top 10 categories by revenue with a horizontal bar chart and direct value labels.
days.revision_checkpoint: When is a box plot misleading, and what would you show instead?

days.concept_explanation: Combine the week: load a raw CSV, clean it, compute two grouped metrics, chart them, and write three sentences that a non-technical reader could act on. The deliverable is the notebook, not the code.
key_takeaways: A notebook is a report; order the cells so it reads top to bottom.
State your cleaning decisions next to the code that makes them.
Every chart needs a one-line takeaway underneath.

resources.title: Jupyter: notebook basics
resources.relevance_note: Short reference for cells, kernels and execution order.

practice_exercises: Pick a public CSV under 5 MB and document three data-quality problems.
Add a markdown cell after each chart with a one-sentence finding.
days.assignment: Submit a notebook that answers one concrete question about the dataset, with two charts and a short written conclusion.
days.revision_checkpoint: If a colleague reran your notebook top to bottom, would they get the same numbers? Why?

capstone_project.title: Dataset investigation notebook
capstone_project.description: Choose a public dataset, ask one question, clean the data, answer the question with two charts and three sentences, and note the limitations of your answer.
deliverables: Notebook that runs top to bottom without errors
Two charts, each with a one-line takeaway

next_steps: Learn SQL so you can pull data without exporting CSVs.
Try scikit-learn on the same dataset to predict one column.
Read about experiment design before trusting any comparison.
